To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

maternal low-protein diet during pregnancy can modulate the expression of genes and proteins that are critical for the regulation of intracellular Ca2+ levels in the neonatal rat heart, and that these alterations in gene and protein expression may contribute to the adverse effects on heart function that are observed in the offspring of the LP diet group.
maternal low-protein diet can induce alterations of the gene and protein expressions of the Ca2+ cycling proteins in the neonate rat heart.
the maternal LP diet induces alterations in the gene and protein expressions of the Ca2+ cycling proteins in the neonate heart.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of maternal protein restriction during pregnancy on Ca2+-catalyzed signaling in the neonatal rat heart.
the mechanisms of fetal programming, and the results may provide a clue as to the pathogenesis of cardiac hypertrophy and/or dysfunction.
the effects of a LP diet in uteros on cardiac function and Ca2+ cycling proteins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
maternal LP diet induces alterations in the Ca2+ cycling gene and protein expression in the heart of neonatal offspring.

a maternal LP diet leads to a reduction in L-type Ca2+ channel and SERCA 2a protein levels and to a reduction in the ratio of phosphorylated PLB/PLB in the neonatal rat heart, which might be responsible for the depressed contractile function in these animals.
maternal LP diet induces changes in Ca2+-cycing protein gene and protein expression in neonatal heart.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fetal heart is a target for the adverse environmental experience of maternal undernutrition.
maternal protein deprivation can induce a shift of Ca2+ cycling in the neonatal hearts from the sarcoplasmic reticulums (SR) to the sarcolemma.

The main takeaway from our work is that

maternal LP diet induces changes in the expression of Ca2+-catalytic and Ca2+-regulatory proteins in the neonate, which may lead to alterations in the Ca2+-handling and contractile function in the adult offspring.
the LP diet can modulate Ca2+-cyclic proteins in the neonate heart, and this may be one of the mechanisms by which an adverse environment can permanently alter cardiac function.
maternal LP diet induces changes in the gene expression of the Ca(2+)-cycling proteins in neonatal hearts, which are associated with changes in their protein levels.
